aliases.name: Abominable Snowman
aliases.meaning: Popularized 1921 by columnist Henry Newman as a translation of metoh-kangmi

aliases.name: Dzu-teh
aliases.meaning: Cattle bear; usually identified with the Himalayan brown bear

description.summary: An ape-like humanoid cryptid said to inhabit the high Himalayas of Nepal, Tibet, Bhutan, and adjacent regions. Central to Sherpa, Tibetan, and Lepcha tradition long before Western contact, the Yeti became a global cryptozoological icon after 20th-century mountaineering expeditions reported tracks and encounters.
description.full: The Yeti is a large, hairy, ape-like creature reported in the snowfields and forested valleys of the Himalayan range. Local Tibetan and Sherpa traditions describe several related beings collectively grouped under the modern term 'Yeti', most commonly the meh-teh (man-bear) and dzu-teh (cattle bear). Western interest accelerated after Eric Shipton's 1951 photographs of large footprints near the Menlung Glacier on the approach to Mount Everest. Several mid-20th-century expeditions, notably Tom Slick's 1957–1959 ventures and the 1960–1961 Hillary–Doig 'Silver Hut' expedition, examined alleged scalps and skins held at Pangboche and Khumjung monasteries. Successive genetic surveys, culminating in Sykes et al. (2014) in Proceedings of the Royal Society B and Lan et al. (2017) in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, identified putative Yeti samples as Himalayan brown bear, Tibetan blue bear, Asiatic black bear, and a domestic dog. Mainstream zoology now treats the Yeti as a folkloric phenomenon with a strong bear-misidentification component, while the figure remains spiritually and culturally important across the Himalayas.

etymology.origin: From Tibetan / Sherpa terms for the creature. 'Yeti' is generally derived from yeh-teh ('that thing') or from a compound of ya ('rocky place') and teh (a softened form of dred, 'bear'). 'Abominable Snowman' was coined by Henry Newman of the Calcutta Statesman in 1921 as a sensational rendering of metoh-kangmi reported by Lt-Col Charles Howard-Bury's Everest reconnaissance.
etymology.meaning: Approximately 'rock-bear' or 'man-bear' depending on derivation; 'metoh-kangmi' translates as 'man-bear of the snow'.
etymology.first_use: 1921 in English-language press (Newman, Calcutta Statesman); local Himalayan terms predate written record

related_phenomena.name: Almas
related_phenomena.description: Caucasus / Central Asian hairy hominid cryptid

related_phenomena.name: Barmanou
related_phenomena.description: Hairy hominid cryptid of the Hindu Kush and Karakoram

features.description: Coarse hair covering the body; reddish-brown or dark in most regional accounts
Walks upright on two legs; some witnesses describe partial quadrupedal movement on steep terrain
Footprints reported in the 30–46 cm range; Shipton's 1951 photograph shows a print roughly 33 cm long with a divergent hallux
Tibetan and Sherpa accounts often describe a conical, sagittal-crested head; the Khumjung 'scalp' has this shape
Reports describe arms reaching the knees, similar to great-ape proportions

physical.morphology: Reports across Himalayan tradition group several distinct forms: the larger dzu-teh (associated by Reinhold Messner and others with the Himalayan brown bear), the man-sized meh-teh (the prototypical humanoid Yeti), and smaller forest-dwelling forms such as the chu-teh (often identified with the Himalayan langur).

abilities.description: Said to range above 4,500 m in snow and ice without difficulty
Sherpa accounts describe a high whistle or hooting call associated with the meh-teh
Folkloric accounts attribute the ability to overpower yaks and other livestock
Said to flee on encountering humans; sightings in monastic record are typically brief

behavior.diet: Folklorically omnivorous; said to take livestock (yaks, sheep) and forage; bear-explanation accounts emphasize plant matter and small mammals
patterns: Reports cluster on glacier approaches and monastery hinterlands
Tracks most often reported in fresh snow above 4,000 m
Direct sightings are rare; most evidence is footprints, hair, or alleged scalps

range.description: The Yeti is reported across the Himalayan and adjacent ranges, particularly in Nepal (Khumbu, Solu, Mustang, Makalu-Barun), the Tibet Autonomous Region of China, Bhutan (where the migoi is the national cryptid), Sikkim and other northern Indian states, and parts of southern Siberia where related 'wild man' traditions exist.

hotspots.name: Menlung Glacier / Everest approach

location.description: Menlung Glacier between Tibet and Nepal, on the approach to Mount Everest

hotspots.notes: Site of Eric Shipton and Michael Ward's 1951 footprint photographs

hotspots.name: Pangboche and Khumjung monasteries

location.description: Pangboche and Khumjung Sherpa villages, Solukhumbu

hotspots.notes: Held alleged Yeti scalps and a hand examined by the Slick (1957–1959) and Hillary (1960–1961) expeditions

hotspots.name: Makalu-Barun Valley

location.description: Barun Valley in the Makalu-Barun National Park

hotspots.notes: Daniel C. Taylor's long-running tracking work, leading to the Asiatic black bear hypothesis (Taylor 2017)

hotspots.name: Zemu Glacier, Sikkim

location.description: Zemu Glacier on the eastern flank of Kangchenjunga

hotspots.notes: Site of N. A. Tombazi's 1925 daylight sighting

first_recorded.source: Tibetan, Sherpa, Lepcha, and Bhutanese oral tradition; Bön ritual references

peak_activity_periods.description: Shipton photographs, Slick expeditions, Hillary–Doig Silver Hut expedition
Successive DNA studies (Sykes 2014; Lan et al. 2017) and the popular re-entry of the Yeti through documentary television

temporal.seasonal_patterns: Track reports concentrate in spring and post-monsoon, when snow is fresh and routes are open.

origins.cultural_roots: The Yeti has deep roots in pre-Buddhist Bön religion and in Tibetan, Sherpa, Lepcha, and Bhutanese oral traditions that long predate Western contact. In Tibetan Buddhism the meh-teh is sometimes treated as a non-human animal capable of moral conduct.
origins.earliest_accounts: B. H. Hodgson, the British Resident at the court of Nepal, described in 1832 a tall, hair-covered creature seen by his servants in northern Nepal — the earliest detailed Western account.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to a Pan-Asian and global 'wild man' tradition: the Bhutanese migoi, the Mongolian almas, the Pakistani barmanou, the Chinese yeren, and the European woodwose.

timeline.event: Tibetan, Sherpa, Lepcha, and Bhutanese traditions of meh-teh, dzu-teh, and migoi
B. H. Hodgson reports a hair-covered bipedal creature in northern Nepal
timeline.source: Hodgson, B. H., Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal

timeline.event: The Howard-Bury Everest reconnaissance reports tracks at ~6,400 m on the Lhakpa La; Henry Newman of the Calcutta Statesman renders metoh-kangmi as 'Abominable Snowman'
timeline.significance: Origin of the English popular term
timeline.source: Howard-Bury, C. K. (1922), Mount Everest: The Reconnaissance, 1921

timeline.event: N. A. Tombazi observes a hair-covered bipedal figure near the Zemu Glacier, Sikkim
Eric Shipton and Michael Ward photograph a large footprint near the Menlung Glacier
timeline.significance: The most-discussed single piece of physical evidence in the Yeti record
timeline.source: Shipton, E. (1952), The Mount Everest Reconnaissance Expedition 1951

timeline.event: The Daily Mail Snowman Expedition led by John Angelo Jackson photographs alleged Yeti scalps and tracks in the Himalayas
Tom Slick funds a series of Yeti expeditions to the Khumbu, with Peter Byrne and others
timeline.significance: Removed and substituted material from the Pangboche 'hand' for analysis
timeline.source: Slick expedition records; Byrne, P., recollections

timeline.event: Edmund Hillary and Marlin Perkins lead the Silver Hut expedition; the Khumjung 'scalp' is taken to the West and identified by Marca Burns and others as serow hide
timeline.significance: First systematic scientific examination of Yeti relics
timeline.source: Hillary, E. & Doig, D. (1962), High in the Thin Cold Air

timeline.event: Reinhold Messner begins fieldwork that he later argues identifies the dzu-teh with the Himalayan brown bear (Ursus arctos isabellinus)
timeline.source: Messner, R. (2000), My Quest for the Yeti

timeline.event: Sykes et al. publish a peer-reviewed genetic survey in Proceedings of the Royal Society B
timeline.significance: First broad peer-reviewed DNA survey of putative Yeti samples

timeline.event: Lan et al. publish a follow-up genetic study in Proceedings of the Royal Society B identifying putative Yeti samples as Himalayan brown bear, Tibetan blue bear, Asiatic black bear, and a domestic dog

history.modern_era: Contemporary Yeti research is dominated by genetic analysis of museum and field-collected hair, claw, and bone samples; by ecological work on Himalayan bears (notably the Asiatic black bear hypothesis of Daniel C. Taylor); and by continued Sherpa, Bhutanese, and Lepcha cultural stewardship of meh-teh and migoi traditions. Bhutan administers the Sakteng Wildlife Sanctuary in part as a migoi reserve.

notable.name: Tombazi sighting, Zemu Glacier

location.description: Near the Zemu Glacier on the eastern flank of Kangchenjunga

types: Royal Geographical Society photographer (N. A. Tombazi)

notable.description: Photographer N. A. Tombazi, on a Royal Geographical Society expedition, reported observing a tall bipedal figure at roughly 200–300 yards on a slope near the Zemu Glacier; the figure pulled at rhododendron bushes and moved on two legs. Tombazi later inspected sixteen footprints, each about 6–7 inches long, in the snow.

credibility.notes: Cited by both pro-Yeti researchers and skeptics as a reference daylight account.

sources: Tombazi, N. A. (1925), Royal Geographical Society lecture

notable.name: Shipton footprint photographs, Menlung Glacier

location.description: Menlung Glacier, on the approach to Mount Everest from the south

credibility_factors: Photographic record with scale ice axe

notable.description: On the 1951 Mount Everest Reconnaissance, Eric Shipton and Michael Ward photographed a line of large footprints in fresh snow at roughly 6,000 m. The lead photograph, with an ice axe for scale, shows a print roughly 33 cm long with a clearly divergent first toe and four smaller digits.

factors: Print interpretation contested between hominid and bear hypotheses
credibility.notes: The single most-analyzed piece of Yeti footprint evidence.

sources: Shipton, E. (1952), The Mount Everest Reconnaissance Expedition 1951

notable.name: Hillary and Tenzing footprint observation

credibility_factors: Lead mountaineers of the first successful Everest ascent

notable.description: During the 1953 British Mount Everest expedition, Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reported observing large footprints in the snow attributed locally to the Yeti. Hillary later organised the 1960–1961 Silver Hut expedition specifically to investigate Yeti claims, and concluded that the evidence was inconsistent with an unknown ape.

credibility.notes: Often cited as the moment in which the Yeti became part of mainstream mountaineering history.

sources: Hillary, E. & Doig, D. (1962), High in the Thin Cold Air

notable.name: Destination Truth footprint cast, Everest region
notable.description: A film crew working on the Sci Fi Channel programme Destination Truth, led by Joshua Gates, photographed and cast a set of three footprints near a streambed in the Everest region. The casts measured roughly 33 cm in length with five toes.

credibility.notes: Often cited in popular accounts; subjected to limited subsequent analysis.

sources: Destination Truth, Sci Fi Channel (2008 broadcast)

physical.name: Pangboche hand
physical.description: An alleged Yeti hand kept at Pangboche monastery in the Khumbu, examined and partially substituted by Peter Byrne during the Slick expeditions and later analyzed in the West.
physical.analysis: Re-examined in 2011 by Edinburgh Zoo geneticists, who reported the sampled bones as human in origin.
physical.source: Royal College of Surgeons archive; BBC reporting (2011)

physical.name: Khumjung 'scalp'
physical.description: Conical hair-covered cap held at Khumjung monastery and brought to the West for analysis under the Hillary–Doig expedition.
physical.analysis: Identified by Marca Burns and others as fashioned from the hide of a Himalayan serow (Capricornis sumatraensis thar).
physical.source: Hillary, E. & Doig, D. (1962), High in the Thin Cold Air

physical.name: Shipton Menlung footprint
physical.description: Photograph of a large footprint in snow on the Menlung Glacier, with an ice axe for scale.
physical.analysis: Variously interpreted as a hominid print, a melt-distorted bear track, or an overlapping double print.

photographic.name: Shipton 1951 footprint photographs
photographic.description: Photographs of a track line in snow on the Menlung Glacier; the lead frame shows a single print at high contrast.
photographic.analysis: Subject of decades of footprint biomechanics debate; cited by both Yeti researchers and skeptics.

trace.name: Sykes et al. 2014 genetic survey
trace.description: Peer-reviewed mitochondrial DNA survey of 30 putative Yeti, Bigfoot, and other anomalous primate hair samples.
trace.analysis: All samples matched known mammals (bears, dogs, cows, raccoons, etc.); two Himalayan samples gave a 100% match to an ancient polar bear / brown bear lineage, later refined as Himalayan brown bear.
trace.source: Sykes, B. C. et al. (2014), Proc. R. Soc. B 281:20140161

trace.name: Lan et al. 2017 Yeti DNA study
trace.description: Peer-reviewed nuclear and mitochondrial sequencing of nine putative Yeti specimens from museum and monastery collections.
trace.analysis: Identified samples as Himalayan brown bear, Tibetan blue bear, Asiatic black bear, and one domestic dog; no anomalous primates.
trace.source: Lan, T. et al. (2017), Proc. R. Soc. B 284:20171804

paranormal.name: Spiritual / supernatural being
paranormal.description: In Tibetan and Bön traditions the meh-teh and migoi are sometimes treated as spiritually charged forest beings whose appearance is an omen rather than a strictly biological event.

scientific.name: Surviving Gigantopithecus blacki
scientific.description: Hypothesis that the Yeti is a relict population of the extinct giant ape Gigantopithecus blacki, surviving in the high Himalayas.
evidence_cited: Geographic plausibility of southern Asian refugia

scientific.name: Undescribed Himalayan hominid
scientific.description: Hypothesis that the meh-teh is an as-yet-undescribed Asian primate species.
evidence_cited: Recent discoveries of large mammal species in remote Asia

skeptical.name: Himalayan brown bear / Tibetan blue bear
skeptical.description: The dzu-teh and many Yeti reports correspond to known Himalayan bear species, especially the rare Himalayan brown bear (Ursus arctos isabellinus) and the Tibetan blue bear (Ursus arctos pruinosus).
evidence_cited: DNA matches in Sykes (2014) and Lan et al. (2017)
Bipedal walking observed in brown bears
Fieldwork by Messner in Tibet and Bhutan

skeptical.name: Asiatic black bear (climbing-track hypothesis)
skeptical.description: Tracks reported as Yeti in forest and snowfield boundary zones are made by Asiatic black bears, whose hind paws step into the prints of their fore paws and whose claws produce a hominid-like track when one paw partially overlies the other.
evidence_cited: Field tracking in the Barun Valley

skeptical.name: Misidentification, hoax, and cultural transmission
skeptical.description: Other Yeti reports are explained by misidentification of langurs, serows, and humans, by deliberate hoaxes (some monastery relics), and by media-driven cultural transmission of expectation.
evidence_cited: Surge in reports following 1950s media coverage

traditions: Tibetan Bön ritual references to mi rgod ('wild man')
Lepcha 'Glacier Being' / God of the Hunt
stories: Monastery custodianship of alleged Yeti scalps and hands at Pangboche and Khumjung
Sherpa accounts of Yeti attacks on yaks and humans recorded by 20th-century expeditions
folklore.beliefs: Across Sherpa, Tibetan, Bhutanese, and Lepcha tradition, the meh-teh / migoi is treated as a real being of the high country, often associated with spiritual significance and avoided rather than hunted.

indigenous.significance: The Yeti and its regional analogues are integrated into long-standing Himalayan knowledge systems about high-altitude ecology, rather than being a strictly cryptozoological category.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: Indigenous Himalayan accounts of meh-teh and migoi predate Western 'Abominable Snowman' framing and should not be conflated with it.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Consult monastic and community authorities before publishing about specific relics, and credit Indigenous sources directly.
